newsitem.title: CHINA: China makes arrests after Xinjiang bombings.
newsitem.headline: China makes arrests after Xinjiang bombings.

text.p: China said on Wednesday it had arrested several suspects in last week's bomb attacks that left nine people dead and 74 wounded in the restive far western region of Xinjiang.
Suspects who planted the bombs on public buses and who sold detonators used in the attacks had been arrested, the official Xinjiang Daily said in a front-page story.
Police were interrogating the suspects and hunting for others still at large, the newspaper said.
It called the bombing attacks a "planned and coordinated act of destruction by a terrorist group".

Three bombs planted on buses blew up within minutes of each other in Xinjiang's capital, Urumqi, on February 25 in an apparently coordinated attack that coincided with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
A fourth bomb failed to explode.
Three people died on the spot, six died later in hospital and 74 people were wounded, an official told Reuters by telephone on Wednesday.
A source has said most of the victims were students on their way home from school.
Moslem separatists want to set up an independent "East Turkestan" in Xinjiang, a region that is home to many Turkic-speaking people, including those of the Uighur ethnic minority.
Exiled Uighur nationalists in neighbouring Kazakhstan on Tuesday claimed responsibility for the bombings and for a similar, previously unreported attack on Monday.
A Chinese government official in Xinjiang denied there had been a new blast on Monday.
Hong Kong's Sing Tao Daily newspaper said on Wednesday that paramilitary and riot police had been sent to reinforce Xinjiang and another frequent flashpoint, the Himalayan region of Tibet.
The Lanzhou Military Region, which oversees Xinjiang, is on alert against further unrest in the oil-rich area, which borders Central Asia, the newspaper said.

Unrest along China's borders, one of Beijing's chief security fears, was highlighted by Premier Li Peng on Saturday in his annual government work report to the National People's Congress, the nation's parliament.
Li did not mention the Xinjiang blasts, which have also been ignored by the official media in Beijing, but vowed to take a tough line on separatism.
In February, an anti-Chinese riot by local Uighurs broke out in Yining in Xinjiang. Chinese officials said nine people were killed.
The riot was one of the largest, most violent demonstrations for independence in Xinjiang since the 1949 communist takeover.

China also faces sporadic outbursts of unrest in Tibet, which has been under tight security since 1959 when troops put down an anti-Chinese uprising and sent the region's spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, fleeing into exile in India.
